It sits at zero on everyday concrete nouns and ordinary narrative prose ('dog', 'table', 'car', 'food', 'house', 'the company was'), so it is the register of the word, not the size or predictability of the next token, that decides.

On the first warm Saturday of spring, Mira wheeled her bicycle to the edge of town, where the market stalls were just opening. The baker stacked loaves in wicker baskets, and a woman in a straw hat sold jars of honey from a folding table. Mira bought two peaches, a carton of milk and a paper bag of walnuts, then sat on the low stone wall to watch the crowd. A boy chased his dog past the fountain, an old man in a green coat tuned a guitar badly, and two girls argued about whose turn it was to hold the rabbit. For a while nothing happened beyond the ordinary business of a market morning: coins changed hands, children whined for sweets, and the church bell rang the half hour.

Then, just past the clock tower, a clerk from the district registry office taped a notice to the lamppost. It stated that the trustees of the Harlow estate had filed a motion to liquidate the remaining assets, that each beneficiary was entitled to submit a claim within ninety days, and that any objection must be lodged with the probate court before the hearing. Mira read it twice. She had worked for old Mrs. Harlow one summer, watering the greenhouse and sorting seed packets, and the word probate seemed far too formal for a woman who had once paid her in jars of jam.

When the bell rang six, the stalls began to fold their awnings and load crates into vans. The honey woman gave Mira an extra jar for helping her carry boxes, and the baker sold the last two loaves for half price. The fountain was switched off, the pigeons settled on the roof of the post office, and the square slowly emptied until only a few bicycles and a dropped glove remained on the cobbles. Mira walked her bike through the gateway, past the notice board with its curling posters for a lost cat and a piano for sale, and turned toward the towpath.

She wheeled the bicycle home along the canal, past the boatyard where the same three hulls had been waiting for paint since autumn. Her brother was on the porch oiling a bicycle chain, and he asked whether she had remembered the milk. She had. They made tea, ate the peaches standing over the sink, and argued mildly about what to plant in the narrow bed beside the fence. Later, when the light went gold, Mira swept the front steps, folded the laundry, and sat with the cat while the boats knocked against the dock.

Across the road, the neighbours were having a late supper on their lawn. Their small daughter ran in circles with a paper kite, and someone laughed loudly at a joke that Mira could not hear. She thought about the notice again, about the long list of names that would have to be written and signed and sent through the post, and about how quickly a summer of watering and sorting could turn into a line in a document. The cat stretched, the light faded, and the market closed behind her without any fuss at all.

At home she put the milk in the fridge, set the peaches in a bowl, and wrote a list on the back of an envelope: milk, thread, stamps, and a note to ask her brother about the fence. The list sat on the table all evening. She read a chapter of her book, listened to the radio, and went to bed early, and by morning she had almost forgotten the notice, though she would remember it years later, when the letter finally arrived and she had to sign her name at the bottom of the page along with everyone else.
